name: Quinine skin lightener

lead: Quinine has been reported as an ingredient in some illegally sold skin-lightening creams, where the aim is a paler, more even complexion. It appears there alongside steroids and mercury compounds.

The reports come from product findings and enforcement records, such as a 1997 Paris police crackdown on illegal trafficking of lightening products. No mechanism for skin lightening is described and no studies of quinine as a lightener were found.

paras: It is not sold as a legitimate lightener. In the reports it is one component of unregulated creams and mixtures, used on the face and body for gradual lightening over repeated applications.

The illicit lightening market is reported to contain hazardous ingredients such as mercury and potent steroids, and regulators in several countries have acted against these products. Quinine-specific harms in this use were not documented in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Quinine has turned up in illicit skin-lightening products sold for a paler, more even complexion, alongside steroids and mercury compounds. Its use for skin tone comes from product reports and enforcement records, and it has not been studied as a lightener.

lead: Quinine has been reported as an ingredient in some skin-lightening products, which people use hoping for a lighter or more even complexion. It is named among substances found in illegal lightening products alongside corticosteroids, mercury compounds and bleach-based preparations; Wikipedia's skin whitening article mentions it in connection with a 1997 Paris police crackdown on illegal trafficking of such products.

Quinine itself is an alkaloid from cinchona bark, used mainly as a malaria medicine and as the bitter flavouring in tonic water. It was isolated by French chemists in 1820 and is prescription-only as a drug in the US, Canada, UK and Australia [1].

No published trial has tested quinine as a skin lightener, and its mechanism in that role is not described in the sources. Wikipedia's quinine article does not mention skin lightening or hyperpigmentation [1].

paras: Skin lightening products have drawn regulatory attention for ingredients including mercury, hydroquinone and potent corticosteroids. The EU banned hydroquinone in cosmetics in 2000, and several countries restrict mercury-containing products, though enforcement varies and such products remain sold online. Quinine appears in the article only as one of the substances found in the illegal market.

Wikipedia notes quinine as a drug can make skin more prone to sunburn (photosensitivity) and can cause rashes, itching, hives and angioedema, with severe reactions such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis reported [1]. Other documented adverse effects include cinchonism (headache, ringing in the ears, vision changes, nausea), low platelets and heart rhythm problems [1]. These relate to quinine as a medicine, not to its use in lightening creams.

timeline.event: French chemists isolate quinine from cinchona bark [1].
Paris police crack down on illegal trafficking of skin-lightening products.
